title: Case Management
intro: The largest exam domain: how a case type is modeled as a lifecycle and then made to move by itself through routing, SLAs, approvals, conditions, child cases, waits and automations. Expect scenario questions that ask which App Studio option (or which Dev Studio rule) satisfies a business requirement.

objectives.objective: Case lifecycle: stages, statuses, and instructions
summary: A case type is the reusable model of a repeatable business transaction, and a case is one running instance of it with its own ID. The lifecycle is organized as **Stages > Processes > Steps**. A stage is a business milestone named with a noun or gerund of no more than two words (it should read naturally in the sentence 'This case is in <Stage>'). Processes and steps are named verb + noun. Every step is either an **assignment** (a person does the work) or an **automation** (the system does the work). Stages can be primary (the happy path) or alternate (exceptions such as cancellation or investigation).

Stage behavior is set in the stage properties: whether the case advances automatically when the stage finishes or waits, and whether finishing the stage resolves the case. You cannot configure transitions on the Create stage. To jump out of sequence (for example into or out of an alternate stage) use a Change Stage automation. The default Create process is a multi-step form: one assignment, one user, several views, with Next/Previous navigation and Submit on the last view. The process option 'Allow users to go back to previous step' adds a Previous button. New processes start in **draft mode**, which lets them run while incomplete; draft mode must be off before production. App Studio clears it automatically when the case type saves without errors, and turning it off by hand is a Dev Studio task.

The case status tells users where a case stands. Standard values are New, Open, Pending-Approval, Pending-Fulfillment, Resolved-Completed, Resolved-Cancelled and Resolved-Rejected. Set a status on a stage (applied on entry; the final stage holds the resolution status) or on an individual step when you need more detail. Reuse existing statuses and keep to about ten or fewer per case type. Instructions belong on steps that need user input. The form shows the step's instructions by default, and you can replace them with custom text or hide them.
keyFacts: Hierarchy: Case Type > Stages > Processes > Steps; a step is an Assignment (human) or an Automation (system).
Stage names: noun or gerund, at most 2 words. Process and step names: verb + noun.
Transitions cannot be configured on the **Create** stage.
The default Create process is a multi-step form: single assignment, single user, multiple views; navigation styles are horizontal, vertical or standard.

Processes are created in draft mode by default. Leaving draft mode on in production is a guardrail violation. App Studio clears it automatically on an error-free save; turning it off manually happens only in Dev Studio.
Standard statuses: New, Open, Pending-Approval, Pending-Fulfillment, Resolved-Completed, Resolved-Cancelled, Resolved-Rejected.
Best practice: no more than 10 statuses per case type, and reuse existing ones.
Status can be set on a Stage (on entry) or on a Step (more specific).
Form views show step instructions by default; override them with custom text or hide them.
In Dev Studio a new case type maps to a Work class and a pyDefault Case Type rule, and each process maps to a Flow rule.

rows: Group of steps; Flow rule in Dev Studio
Where the case stands; set on stage or step

examTraps: Stage names that are actions ('Review application') are wrong; actions belong to processes and steps.
You cannot set transitions, SLAs or escalations on the Create stage.
Draft mode is ON by default, not off. App Studio turns it off automatically; only Dev Studio turns it off manually.
Creating a new custom status when a standard one fits goes against best practice.

objectives.objective: Service level agreements: urgency, goal, deadline, and passed deadline
summary: An SLA (called 'Goal & deadline' in App Studio) sets time milestones and raises urgency as each one passes. The **goal** is when the work should ideally be done, the **deadline** is when it becomes late, and the **passed deadline** repeats after the deadline, either a fixed number of times or until the work completes. Goal and deadline are measured from the start of the work and fire once each. Passed deadline can only be configured in Dev Studio on the SLA rule. Urgency ranges from 0 to 100. Each milestone can add 1 to 100. Once urgency reaches 100, further increments are ignored but escalation actions still run.

SLAs can sit at the case type level (from creation or reopening until resolution), the stage level (entry to exit), the process level (start until the last step finishes), and on assignment (Collect Information) and approval steps. You cannot put an SLA or escalation on the Create stage. In the case type Settings tab > Goal & deadline you choose Use SLA: Custom, Existing or Never, and Calculate time from start of: This Case, Parent Case or Top-level Case, with durations in days plus HH:MM:SS. App Studio creates a Dev Studio SLA rule behind the scenes. An existing SLA rule shows in the App Studio list only if it is marked as a relevant record.

Case urgency and assignment urgency are different values. A new assignment starts at the case urgency, and the initial case urgency is set on the case type Settings tab (default 10, set by the Work- pyDefault data transform). Stage and process SLAs change case urgency. Changing case urgency affects only assignments created afterward, not existing ones. Worklists and work queues are ordered by urgency, and Get Next Work picks the most urgent assignment. App Studio escalations can notify the case creator or participants. Dev Studio adds advanced options: initial urgency, delay timers, variable interval length, a business-day calendar, and escalation actions beyond notification such as reassigning the work or resolving the case.
keyFacts: Urgency range is 0 to 100. Default initial case urgency is 10. Each milestone adds 1 to 100.
At urgency 100, further increments are ignored but escalation actions still run.
Goal and deadline fire once each. Passed deadline repeats a fixed number of times or until the work completes.
Passed deadline is configured **only in Dev Studio** on the SLA rule.
Example: start 10, goal +10 gives 20, deadline +10 gives 30.
SLA levels: case type, stage, process, assignment step, approval step. Not allowed on the Create stage.
Use SLA: Custom / Existing / Never. Calculate from: This Case / Parent Case / Top-level Case.
Changing case urgency affects only new assignments, not existing ones.
Get Next Work returns the highest-urgency assignment first.
Reassigning or resolving the case as an escalation action is a Dev Studio SLA option; App Studio escalations notify (creator or participants).

rows: Repeats N times or until done

examTraps: Urgency cannot go above 100, but escalations keep running after it gets there.
Raising case urgency does not re-rank assignments that already exist.
Passed deadline is not in the App Studio Goal & deadline panel.
'Calculate time from Parent/Top-level case' is how a child case SLA can be measured from an ancestor's start.

objectives.objective: Routing assignments to users, work groups, work queues, and by business logic
modules: Creating and managing teams of users
summary: Each assignment must be routed to someone. The options are the **current user**, a **specific user** (the assignment goes to that person's worklist), a **work queue** (a shared list for a team), or **business logic** (conditions pick the destination, for example sending recreational-vehicle loans to an RV underwriters queue). Worklists and work queues both list open assignments in urgency order. An assignment in a work queue stays there until a team member pulls it or a manager sends it to someone.

In App Studio a team is a work group, and in Dev Studio a user is an operator. A work group is a cross-functional team with a manager and exactly one work queue. A work queue needs a work group and a work group needs a work queue. The default queue is default@<org>. Every operator must belong to at least one work group and can belong to several. The work group manager is used for notifications, approvals, routing and escalations, and works from the Web Portal. **Authorized managers** can help transfer assignments and do not have to be work group members. They cannot perform approvals, and if they are outside the group they cannot complete its work-queue assignments. In Dev Studio a decision table can act as a router, and routing to a queue updates the Assign-Workbasket assignment.
keyFacts: Four routing options: current user, specific user (worklist), work queue, business logic (conditions).
Worklist = an operator's own assignments. Work queue = shared assignments for a team.
Each work group has a manager and **exactly one** work queue; neither can exist without the other.
Default work queue: default@<org>.
An operator must belong to at least one work group and can belong to many.
Work-queue items stay until a member pulls them or a manager sends them.
Authorized managers can transfer assignments, need not be members, cannot approve, and cannot complete work-queue assignments if outside the group.
Terminology: Team = Work Group, User = Operator.
Best practice is to configure people in App Studio; use Dev Studio for advanced items such as permissions.

rows: The person doing the work continues
One named person must do it
Any qualified team member can pick it up
The destination depends on case data

examTraps: Authorized managers are not approvers.
A work group has one work queue, not several.
Routing to a work queue does not put the work on anyone's worklist until it is pulled or sent.

objectives.objective: Approvals, including cascading approvals with a reporting structure or an authority matrix
summary: The Approve/Reject step routes like any assignment (user, work queue or business logic) and supports email approval and mobile approval, so approvers can respond without opening the application. On **approve**, the case continues or changes to a specific stage, and you can optionally set a status. On **reject**, the case resolves (default status Resolved-Rejected), continues, or changes stage.

Choosing the Cascading option creates a chain of approvals. A **reporting structure** cascade reads the operator ID record and uses either the Reporting Manager or the Workgroup Manager. The number of approvers can be One, All (the whole hierarchy), or Custom (levels decided by When rules, for example amount thresholds). An **authority matrix** is more flexible and is the right choice when at least one approver is outside the reporting structure. Its approver list is filled by a decision table, data page, activity or data transform, and approvals run in list order. If you use a decision table it must be set to **Evaluate all rows**, otherwise it returns only one result. Among decision rules, only decision tables (not decision trees) can drive an authority matrix.
keyFacts: Approve: continue, or change to a specific stage; optionally set a status.
Reject: resolve (default Resolved-Rejected), continue, or change stage.
Email approval and mobile approval let approvers act outside the application.
Reporting structure uses the operator record: Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager.
Reporting structure approver count: One, All, or Custom (When rules and thresholds).
Authority matrix: use when at least one approver is outside the reporting chain.
Authority matrix sources: Decision table, Data Page, Activity, or Data Transform.
A decision table feeding an authority matrix must use Evaluate all rows; approvals happen in list order.
Decision trees cannot drive an authority matrix.

rows: Operator record (Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager)
A list built by a DT, data page, activity or data transform
Approvals that go up the management chain
Approvers outside the chain (e.g. Legal, Finance)
Every entry in the list, in order

examTraps: Choosing authority matrix when every approver is in the manager chain; reporting structure is simpler.
Forgetting Evaluate all rows, so only one approver is returned.
Picking a decision tree for an authority matrix.
Assuming rejection always resolves the case; it can also continue or change stage.

summary: The **Search duplicate Cases** automation step compares the current case with existing cases in two passes. First, **basic conditions** filter candidates: a case must match ALL of them to be considered, and you can cap how many candidates are returned. Next, each candidate is scored with **weighted conditions**, each worth 1 to 100. If the total meets or exceeds the threshold, the case is a potential duplicate.

If potential duplicates are found, a user reviews them and either resolves the current case as a duplicate (status Resolved-Duplicate) or ignores the matches and continues. If nothing matches, the case continues automatically. For example: date of birth as a basic condition, four weighted conditions of 25 each, and a threshold of 50, so any two weighted matches on a same-birthdate case flag it.
keyFacts: Implemented with the Search duplicate Cases automation step.
Basic conditions: ALL must match for a case to be a candidate; you can limit the number of candidates.
Weighted conditions: each weight is 1 to 100; candidate is a potential duplicate when the sum is at least the threshold.
Resolving as a duplicate sets the status to Resolved-Duplicate.
The user can also ignore the matches and continue.
No matches: the case simply continues.

rows: Weights 1 to 100; sum compared with threshold

examTraps: A case that matches every weighted condition but fails a basic condition is never a candidate.
The threshold check is 'at least' the threshold, so equal counts as a match.
Duplicates are not resolved automatically; a user decides.

objectives.objective: Optional actions in the case lifecycle and for data objects
modules: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
summary: Optional actions are work users can start whenever they need to, outside the planned steps. A **user action** is a single step or screen, and an **optional process** is several steps. Either can be **case-wide** (available in every stage) or limited to one **stage**. Edit details and Change Stage are built-in case-wide actions. Configure them with the Optional Actions button in the upper-right of the Workflow tab; at runtime users open them from the Actions menu. Data objects also support an Update Details action so users can change only the information they need, with validation and pre/post-processing.

The **promoted action** appears as a button (on the case header, in the summary panel) so users do not have to open the Actions menu. It is the first stage-wide action other than Edit details, or if there is none, the first case-wide action. Only user actions can be promoted, not optional processes.
keyFacts: User action = single step/screen. Optional process = multi-step.
Scope: case-wide or stage-only.
Built-in case-wide actions: Edit details and Change Stage.
Configured with the Optional Actions button (upper-right of the Workflow tab); run from the Actions menu.
Promoted action = first stage-wide action other than Edit details; otherwise the first case-wide action.
Only user actions can be promoted; optional processes cannot.
Data objects offer an Update Details action for targeted updates.
Change Stage is useful for moving into or out of alternate stages.
examTraps: Adding the same step to every stage when a case-wide optional action does the job.
Expecting an optional process to show as the promoted button.
Edit details is skipped when the promoted action is chosen from the stage actions.

objectives.objective: Using conditions to automate workflow decisions
modules: Skipping a Process or a Stage
summary: Conditions let the case decide its own path from data. A condition is a field, a comparator and a value, and several conditions combine with AND. They are used in decision shapes (the orange diamond in the Process Modeler) to choose a branch, which can also leave the stage through Change Stage. They are also used in business-logic routing, custom approval levels, and stage and process skip rules. A When rule answers a single yes/no question. When several properties together determine an outcome, use a decision table. A decision shape that references a decision table automatically gets one connector per possible result.

Values that change often should not be hard-coded. Configuration settings (which replace Dynamic System Settings) can hold parameters such as an approval monetary limit and are referenced through the Condition Builder. Delegated decision tables let process owners make small production changes, such as lowering a threshold, without a developer.
keyFacts: Condition = field + comparator + value; multiple conditions are ANDed.
Decision shape (orange diamond) creates conditional paths and can go to another stage via Change Stage.
When rule = yes/no; decision table = outcome depends on several properties.
A decision shape referencing a DT auto-adds one connector per result.
Configuration settings replace DSS and are referenced through the Condition Builder (for example an approval monetary limit).
Delegated decision tables let business owners change values in production (e.g. a threshold from $500 to $400).
Custom levels in reporting-structure approvals are decided with When rules.
examTraps: Hard-coding a business threshold that the business wants to change itself.
Using a When rule where the result depends on many inputs and needs more than yes/no.
Choosing Dynamic System Settings; configuration settings are their replacement.

summary: A flow action defines what a user can do at a step. In App Studio flow actions are called user actions. A flow action is attached either to a connector or to an assignment shape. A **connector action** completes the assignment and moves the flow forward. A **local action** updates the assignment without advancing it, and is configured in the assignment properties.

Flow actions are also where step-level logic hooks in. Validate rules are assigned to flow actions. Pre- and post-processing can run data transforms (for example copying a shipping address to billing) or save a savable data page. A Validate rule can be qualified by flow action, so the same field can have different validation on different forms. Flow actions can be marked as relevant records so App Studio can reuse them.
keyFacts: Flow action = what a user can do at an assignment; called a User action in App Studio.
Connector action: completes the assignment and advances the flow.
Local action: updates the assignment without advancing; configured in assignment properties.
Validate rules are assigned to flow actions.
Pre/post-processing on a flow action can run a data transform or trigger a savable data page.
Flow actions (user actions) are a relevant-record rule type.
examTraps: A local action never moves the case forward.
Validation for a single screen belongs to the flow action, not the property definition.

objectives.objective: Pausing and resuming processing with wait steps
summary: A Wait automation step pauses a process until something happens. A **Timer** wait resumes after a set date/time interval or at a date/time stored in a property. A **Case Dependency** wait makes a parent case wait until all or any child cases of a chosen type reach a status, or reach 'To be resolved' (any status starting with Resolved).

Case dependency options include whether to consider the child's current status or only changes made after the parent reaches the wait, and whether a user may cancel the wait. The child cases must already exist when the parent reaches the wait step; otherwise the wait is skipped. A wait step is different from a case simply sitting at an assignment until a user acts.
keyFacts: Two wait types: Timer and Case Dependency (case status).
Timer: set a date/time interval, or reference a date/time property.
Case Dependency: all or any child cases of a type reach a status, or 'To be resolved'.
'To be resolved' = any status beginning with Resolved.
Options: consider current status vs only changes after reaching the wait; allow user to cancel the wait.
Children must be created before the wait step, otherwise the wait is skipped.
A wait step is not the same as waiting on a user assignment.

rows: The date/time in a field is reached
All/any child cases of a type reach a status or are resolved

examTraps: If the children already resolved before the parent arrives and you chose only changes after reaching the wait, the parent may never resume.
Creating child cases after the wait step means the wait is skipped.
Using an SLA goal as a pause; SLAs raise urgency and escalate, they do not hold the flow.

objectives.objective: Skipping a stage or process based on conditions
modules: Skipping a Process or a Stage
summary: Stages and processes can be conditional, and their defaults are opposite. A **stage** is never skipped unless you add a 'Skip stage when' condition. A **process** always starts unless you add a 'Start process when' condition. Each condition is a field, comparator and value, and multiple conditions are combined with AND, so all must be true.

Use a skip rule when whole parts of the lifecycle do not apply to some cases, such as skipping an inspection stage for low-value claims or running a reference-check process only for senior hires. If you instead need to jump to a specific stage from the middle of a flow, use a Change Stage automation or a decision shape.
keyFacts: Stage default: never skipped. Configure 'Skip stage when'.
Process default: always starts. Configure 'Start process when'.
Condition = field + comparator + value; multiple conditions are ANDed.
For a stage you describe when to SKIP; for a process you describe when to RUN.
Change Stage automation moves the case to a named stage out of sequence.
examTraps: The logic is inverted between stage (skip when) and process (start when).
Multiple conditions are AND, not OR.

summary: A top-level case has no parent. A child case is work that must be completed to resolve the parent, and it lets work run in parallel. The parent cannot resolve until its children do. Use child cases when work is done by different parties, needs separate reporting, runs on a different time frame, or is common to several case types (for example a reusable Body Injury case). In the class hierarchy a child case type sits under the parent's work class.

Create children with the Create Case automation step. Dev Studio adds options such as creating a top-level case instead of a child and creating multiple child cases. When passing data, decide between a **snapshot copy** at creation (fine for data that won't change, such as accident details) and **referencing the parent's data** when it must stay in sync (such as a travel itinerary). Referencing is an advanced Dev Studio configuration. Related tools: the Wait step (case dependency), Update a Case (current case or all child/descendant cases), SLAs calculated from the Parent or Top-level case, and the Related Cases widget.
keyFacts: Top-level case = no parent. A parent waits for its children before it resolves.
Reasons: different parties, separate reporting, different time frames, reuse across case types, parallel processing.
Created with the Create Case automation step.
Dev Studio options: top-level vs child, and multiple child cases.
Data propagation copies a snapshot at creation; referencing parent data keeps it synchronized (Dev Studio advanced).
The child case type class sits under the parent's class (e.g. Laptop Request under IT Ticket).
Update a Case automation can update the current case or all child/descendant cases.

rows: Always reads the parent's current values

examTraps: Propagated data does not update in the child when the parent changes.
Child cases are for separate units of work, not just for grouping screens.
Parallel processing for a distinct unit of work suggests a child case, not more steps in the parent.

modules: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
summary: Automation steps let the system do work without a person, which saves time and reduces errors. Add them from a step with More > Automations, or in the Process Modeler with Add > Automations. App Studio automations include: Attach content, Change to a Stage, Change to next Stage, Change to previous Stage, Connect Generative AI, Create Case, Create PDF (needs a workaround in Constellation), Generate document, Persist Case (makes a temporary case permanent), Post to Pulse, Push notification, Run Data Transform, Send email, Send notification (multiple channels), Update a Case (current or all child/descendant cases), Search duplicate Cases, Wait (timer or case status), and Questionnaire. A Save Data Page step writes data back to a system of record.

In the Process Modeler, Start is a green circle, End a red circle, an assignment a green rectangle, a subprocess such as Approve/Reject a blue rectangle, an automation a yellow rectangle, and a decision an orange diamond. Automation steps do not get a form view; one is generated automatically only for user steps.
keyFacts: Add via Step > More > Automations, or Process Modeler Add > Automations.
Persist Case turns a temporary case into a permanent one.
Run Data Transform copies or sets data (e.g. shipping address to billing).
Send notification targets multiple channels; Send email sends email only.
Update a Case works on the current case or all child/descendant cases.
Wait pauses on a timer or a case status.
Create PDF needs a workaround in Constellation.
Shapes: Start green circle, End red circle, Assignment green rectangle, Subprocess blue rectangle, Automation yellow rectangle, Decision orange diamond.
No form view is generated for automation steps.
examTraps: Create Case makes a new (child) case; Persist Case keeps an existing temporary case.
Send email vs Send notification: only Send notification covers several channels.
Change to a Stage goes to a named stage; Change to next/previous Stage is relative.

summary: A **decision table** checks the same set of properties across many combinations. Each column is a property or expression, and rows are evaluated top to bottom; the first row whose conditions are all true returns its result. An Otherwise row at the bottom guarantees a result. Setting **Evaluate all rows** (Results tab) returns every matching row instead, which an authority matrix needs, and disables 'Allowed to return values'. A table built in App Studio becomes a DT rule in the Work- class. A Dev Studio table must be marked as a relevant record before App Studio users can use it. Delegation lets process owners make small production changes, and delegation options on the Results tab control what they can change (for example add columns but not rows). Decision tables can also drive flow decision shapes and assignment routing.

A **decision tree** is a set of branches, each with a comparison value, operator and action (return, continue, or evaluate a nested branch), checked top-down with an otherwise value. Use a tree when different properties matter on different branches or when conditions depend on each other. Use a table when the same properties apply everywhere. The wrong choice shows up as a table full of empty cells or a tree full of repeated conditions. **Show conflicts** flags rows or branches that can never be reached (for example 'Score > 900' above 'Score > 1000'); conflicts appear as warnings on save and on the Guardrails landing page, and none are shown when Evaluate all rows is on. **Show completeness** adds rows for missing combinations, which can produce many rows that you decide whether to keep.
keyFacts: DT rows are evaluated top to bottom; the first row with all conditions true wins.
An Otherwise result guarantees a return value.
Evaluate all rows returns all matches, disables 'Allowed to return values', and is required for an authority matrix.
Only decision tables (not trees) support authority-matrix cascading approvals.
Table = same properties in many combinations. Tree = different properties or nested, dependent conditions.
Show conflicts finds unreachable rows/branches; warnings appear on save and on the Guardrails landing page.
Show completeness adds rows for missing conditions.
App Studio DTs are created in the Work- class; Dev Studio DTs need relevant-record marking for App Studio use.
Delegation lets business owners change values in production; Results tab controls what they can change.
Trees can be referenced from flows, Declare Expressions, activities and routers.

rows: Different properties per branch, nested logic
Rows top to bottom, first full match

examTraps: A broad condition placed above a narrower one hides it; Show conflicts flags the narrower row.
Show completeness adds rows; it does not remove conflicts.
Turning on Evaluate all rows suppresses conflict reporting.
A Dev Studio DT is invisible in App Studio until it is marked as a relevant record.

summary: A persona is the business view of a type of user, managed in App Studio under Users > User Management > Personas tab. The default persona is 'Users'. Creating a persona also creates default permissions, a work queue and an access group (creating an access group does not create a persona). Each persona maps to a role (configured in Dev Studio), but not every role has a persona. Users are invited by email and given a persona or a developer role, and generic shared accounts such as 'admin' should not be used. Autopilot can suggest personas.

In the lifecycle's Personas & Channels section you can draft which personas use which channels in each stage and plan them into releases. Drafting does not configure access: by default a persona can reach all pages. To restrict a portal, assign the persona when you configure the portal (for example a Manager Portal). Several personas can share one channel interface.
keyFacts: Managed in App Studio: Users > User Management > Personas tab. Default persona: 'Users'.
Creating a persona creates default permissions, a work queue and an access group; not the reverse.
Each persona has a role, but not every role has a persona.
Persona and channel access can be set per stage; personas can share channels.
Drafting persona/channel mapping in the lifecycle does NOT restrict access; personas see all pages by default.
Restrict a portal by assigning personas when configuring the portal.
Users are invited by email with a persona or developer role; avoid generic accounts like admin.
examTraps: Assuming the lifecycle Personas & Channels draft enforces security.
Thinking an access group created in Dev Studio creates a persona.
Persona = business alignment; role = specific permissions. They are not the same object.

questions.stem: In a Loan Application case type, applicants flagged during intake must move straight to a Fraud Review alternate stage. The architect opens the Create stage's properties to set up this transition. Which statement about this plan is correct?
options: A Change to a Stage step cannot target an alternate stage.
The Create stage transition must be set to resolve on stage completion.
Stage transitions cannot be configured on the Create stage.
Alternate stages can be entered only through a Create stage transition.
questions.explanation: Pega does not let you configure a transition on the Create stage, so this plan fails; the usual way to reach an alternate stage is a Change to a Stage automation, which works to and from alternate stages. Resolving on stage completion is a setting for other stages, not something the Create stage requires. Alternate stages are not tied to the Create stage. Saying Change to a Stage cannot target an alternate stage reverses the fact.

questions.stem: In a Warranty Claim case type, the Repair stage shows Open. While the 'Await parts' step is active, the case must show Pending-Fulfillment. Which two statements about this design are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Set the Pending-Fulfillment status on the Await parts step.
A status set on a Stage is applied when the case enters the stage.
Create a custom status, because Pending statuses are reserved for approvals.
A status set on a Stage is applied when the stage's last step completes.
questions.explanation: Status can be set on a Stage or on a Step, and the Step setting is the more specific one, so the Await parts step should set Pending-Fulfillment. A Stage status takes effect when the case enters the stage. Pending-Fulfillment is a standard status, and best practice is to reuse existing statuses rather than create new ones. The claim that a Stage status applies when the last step completes has the timing wrong: it applies on stage entry, and only the final stage supplies a resolution status.

questions.stem: Several processes in the Onboarding case type still have unconfigured steps, and go-live is two weeks away. Which two statements about draft mode are correct? (Choose Two)
options: App Studio turns off draft mode when the case type saves without errors.
Draft mode must be off before production, or a guardrail violation results.
Draft mode stops a process from running until its configuration is complete.
Draft mode can be turned off manually only in App Studio.
questions.explanation: Processes are created in draft mode, and leaving it on in production is a guardrail violation. App Studio turns draft mode off by itself once the case type saves with no errors. Draft processes still run even when their configuration is incomplete, which is the point of draft mode. Turning draft mode off by hand is done in Dev Studio, not App Studio.

questions.stem: A Permit case type starts at urgency 10. Its SLA adds 10 at the goal and 20 at the deadline. A passed deadline in Dev Studio adds 15 and repeats 5 times. Which statement describes an unresolved case after the SLA finishes?
options: Urgency is 115, because SLA increments are not capped.
Urgency is 100, and escalation actions stopped once urgency hit 100.
Urgency is 100, and escalation actions still ran at every interval.
Urgency is 55, because the passed deadline adds its value only once.
questions.explanation: 10 + 10 + 20 + (15 x 5) = 115, but urgency cannot go above 100. Once urgency reaches 100, further increments are ignored, but escalation actions still run at each interval. The 115 answer ignores the cap. Saying escalations stop at 100 confuses the urgency cap with escalation behavior. A passed deadline repeats a fixed number of times or until the work is complete, so it does not add its value only once.

questions.stem: A Permit review must warn reviewers at 2 days, be treated as late at 4 days, and then escalate daily until the review is completed. Which two statements about configuring this are correct? (Choose Two)
options: The goal and the deadline are both measured from the start of the SLA.
The passed deadline is measured from the goal and occurs only once.
The daily escalation is a passed deadline, set on the SLA rule in Dev Studio.
The deadline can be set to repeat a fixed number of times in App Studio.
questions.explanation: A passed deadline repeats, either a fixed number of times or until the work completes, and you configure it only on the SLA rule in Dev Studio. The goal (2 days) and the deadline (4 days) are each measured from the start and each happens once. The passed deadline follows the deadline, not the goal, and it repeats. The deadline does not repeat, and App Studio cannot configure repeating escalation.

questions.stem: Case CL-88 has an open Review assignment with urgency 10. A stage SLA then reaches its goal and raises the case urgency to 30. Which statement is correct?
options: Stage SLAs change assignment urgency only, not case urgency.
The Review assignment is raised to 30 immediately.
New assignments always start at the case type's initial urgency.
The Review assignment stays at 10; new assignments start at 30.
questions.explanation: An assignment's initial urgency is copied from the case urgency, and a change to case urgency affects only assignments created afterward. So the open Review assignment keeps 10 and new ones start at 30. Existing assignments are not updated. Stage and Process SLA adjustments change the case urgency, so the claim that they change only assignment urgency is backwards. New assignments take the current case urgency, not the initial value from the Settings tab.

questions.stem: An architect is adding SLAs to a Travel Request case type. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: A case-level SLA runs from creation or reopening until resolution.
An SLA cannot be set on the Create stage.
A process SLA runs from stage entry until the case leaves the stage.
Escalation can be set on the Create stage even though an SLA cannot.
questions.explanation: The case type SLA runs from when the case is created or reopened until it is resolved. The Create stage cannot have an SLA. Stage entry to stage exit describes a Stage SLA; a Process SLA runs from when the process is called until its last step is done. The Create stage cannot have escalation either, so the option that allows escalation there is only half right.

questions.stem: Policy case POL-12 creates Claim child cases, and each Claim creates Payment child cases. Every Payment SLA must be measured from when POL-12 started. Which Goal & deadline setting should the Payment case type use?
options: Calculate time from start of: This Case
Use SLA: Existing, pointing to the Policy SLA
Calculate time from start of: Parent Case
Calculate time from start of: Top-level Case
questions.explanation: POL-12 has no parent, so it is the top-level case, and Top-level Case measures each Payment from POL-12's start. Parent Case would use the Claim, which is the Payment's direct parent. This Case would start timing when each Payment begins. Use SLA: Existing picks which SLA rule to reuse; it does not change the point that time is measured from.

questions.stem: When the Underwriting assignment misses its deadline, it must be reassigned to a supervisor and the case participants must be notified. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: App Studio can notify the case Participants when the milestone is reached.
Escalation actions stop running once case urgency reaches 100.
App Studio escalation can reassign the work or resolve the case directly.
Reassigning the work is an extra escalation action configured in Dev Studio.
questions.explanation: In App Studio, escalation notifies the Creator or the Participants. Reassigning work and resolving the case are extra escalation actions that are only available in Dev Studio. Escalation actions keep running after urgency hits 100; only the urgency increments stop.

questions.stem: Six appraisers share the 'Inspect property' step. Any of them may do it, and each one pulls the next item when free. How should the step be routed?
options: To the current user
To the work group manager's worklist
To the Appraisal team's work queue
To a specific user chosen by business logic
questions.explanation: A work queue is shared by a work group, and an assignment stays there until a member pulls it, which is exactly this requirement. Routing to the current user keeps the work with whoever is processing the case. The manager's worklist is personal to the manager. Business logic is for routing based on conditions, and sending to one specific user does not let the whole team pull from a shared pool.

questions.stem: An architect is setting up teams for a Claims application. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Each work group has a manager and exactly one work queue.
An operator must belong to at least one work group.
The default work queue can exist without any work group.
An operator can belong to only one work group at a time.
questions.explanation: A work group is a cross-functional team with a manager and exactly one work queue. Every operator must belong to at least one work group, and can belong to several. A work queue always needs a work group, including the default queue.

questions.stem: Lena is an authorized manager of the Billing work group but is not a member of it. Which action can Lena perform?
options: Transfer Billing assignments to other users
Approve Billing cases routed to the work group manager
Complete assignments taken from the Billing work queue
Act as a cascading approver for Billing members
questions.explanation: Authorized managers help transfer assignments and do not have to be work group members. They cannot perform approvals, which rules out both approval options. Because Lena is outside the work group, she cannot complete work queue assignments either.

questions.stem: A work queue holds ASG-1 (urgency 45) and ASG-2 (urgency 70). A stage SLA then raises the case urgency of ASG-1's case to 80. A user clicks Get Next Work. Which assignment is returned, and why?
options: ASG-1, because it entered the work queue first
Either one, because Get Next Work ignores urgency
ASG-1, because its case urgency is now 80
ASG-2, because ASG-1's assignment urgency is still 45
questions.explanation: Get Next Work returns the assignment with the highest urgency. A change to case urgency affects only new assignments, so ASG-1 stays at 45 and ASG-2 (70) comes first. Reading the case urgency instead of the assignment urgency is the trap. Get Next Work orders by urgency, not by time in the queue, and it does not ignore urgency.

questions.stem: Expense reports under $5,000 need the requester's manager. From $5,000, the manager's manager must also approve. Above $25,000, one more level is needed. All approvers are in the reporting line. Which configuration fits?
options: Three single-level Approve/Reject steps routed to a work queue
Cascading, reporting structure, number of approvers Custom with When rules
Cascading, reporting structure, number of approvers All
Cascading, authority matrix populated by a decision tree
questions.explanation: All approvers are in the reporting line, so use a reporting structure. Custom lets When rules and thresholds decide how many levels approve. All would send every report up the whole hierarchy. An authority matrix is for approvers outside the reporting structure, and it does not support decision trees. Approve/Reject steps routed to a work queue ignore the reporting line.

questions.stem: Contract CT-310 must be approved by Legal counsel and then by the Finance controller. Neither is in the requester's reporting line. Which two statements about the configuration are correct? (Choose Two)
options: The approvers act in parallel, whatever their order in the list.
A decision table that populates the matrix must evaluate all rows.
Use a cascading approval based on an authority matrix.
A decision tree can populate the matrix if it returns a list.
questions.explanation: An authority matrix handles approvers outside the reporting structure. If a decision table builds the matrix, it must evaluate all rows; otherwise it returns only one approver. Approvals happen in list order, not in parallel. Authority matrix approvals support only decision tables, so a decision tree is not an option.

questions.stem: An architect adds an Approve/Reject step to a Purchase Request case type and keeps the default rejection behavior. What happens when the approver rejects the request?
options: The case returns to the previous stage for rework.
The case is resolved with the status Resolved-Cancelled.
The case is resolved with the status Resolved-Rejected.
The case continues to the next step with a Pending status.
questions.explanation: By default, rejection resolves the case as Resolved-Rejected. Continuing or changing to another stage are options you must configure; they are not the default. Resolved-Cancelled is a standard status, but rejection does not use it.

questions.stem: In Purchase Request PR-310, a manager approval step is being configured. Which two configurations are available? (Choose Two)
options: Route the approval to a specific user, but not to a work queue.
On approval, change to a specific stage and set a status.
Let the approver approve from an email outside the application.
On rejection, the case must always be resolved.
questions.explanation: On approval, the case can continue or change to a specific stage, optionally setting a status. Email and mobile approval let the approver act from outside the app. On rejection, the case can be resolved, continue or change stage, so it does not always resolve. Approval routing supports a user, a work queue or business logic.

questions.stem: A reporting-structure cascading approval is set to use the Workgroup Manager. Where does Pega find the first approver?
options: From a decision table set to evaluate all rows
From the requester's operator ID record and work group
From the work queue that the approval step is routed to
From the case's Interested participants
questions.explanation: Reporting-structure approvals read the operator ID record, using either the Reporting Manager or the Workgroup Manager. Routing to a work queue is a different routing choice. Decision tables that evaluate all rows belong to authority matrices. Interested participants follow a case but do not process it.

questions.stem: A Search duplicate Cases step uses Date of birth as its basic condition. Weighted conditions: last name 30, phone 20, email 25, postal code 25. The threshold is 50. Case A has the same DOB and matches phone and postal code. Case B has a different DOB and matches all four. Case C has the same DOB and matches last name and phone. Which cases are flagged?
options: Cases A, B and C
Case C only
Cases A and C
Cases B and C
questions.explanation: A case must meet every basic condition before its weights count, so Case B is out despite matching all four weighted conditions. Case A scores 20 + 25 = 45, which is below 50. Case C scores 30 + 20 = 50, which meets the threshold.

questions.stem: A Search duplicate Cases step in claim CL-204 finds a potential duplicate. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: The user can ignore the match and continue processing CL-204.
The earlier matching case is resolved as Resolved-Duplicate.
The user can resolve CL-204 as a duplicate, giving it Resolved-Duplicate.
CL-204 is resolved automatically once the threshold is met.
questions.explanation: Once a potential duplicate is found, the user reviews it and either resolves the current case as Resolved-Duplicate or ignores the match and continues. The step does not resolve the case on its own. The resolution applies to the current case, CL-204, not to the earlier case it matched.

questions.stem: Claims with different policy numbers must never be treated as duplicates, whatever else matches. How should the policy number be used in the Search duplicate Cases step?
options: As a Skip stage when condition on the stage
As a basic condition
As a weighted condition worth 100
As the duplicate threshold value
questions.explanation: Every basic condition must match before a case can be a candidate, so a basic condition on policy number excludes all other policies. A weighted condition only adds to a score, so other matches can still reach the threshold without it. The threshold is a number to compare scores against, not a field. Skipping the stage turns off the whole check instead of excluding mismatched cases.

questions.stem: In the Inspection stage, the stage-only actions are, in order: optional process 'Request reinspection', user action 'Log photo', user action 'Update contact'. Case-wide actions are Edit details and Change Stage. Which is the promoted action in Inspection?
options: Edit details
Log photo
Change Stage
Request reinspection
questions.explanation: The promoted action is the first stage action other than Edit details, but only user actions can be promoted, not optional processes. Request reinspection is an optional process, so Log photo is the first eligible action. Case-wide actions are used only when no stage action qualifies.

questions.stem: Agents must update a customer's phone number on one screen at any point in a Service case. During the Investigation stage only, they must be able to run a multi-step escalation review. Which two configurations meet this? (Choose Two)
options: A stage-only optional process for the escalation review
A case-wide optional process for the phone update
A case-wide user action for the phone update
A stage-only user action for the escalation review
questions.explanation: A single-screen action is a user action, and it is case-wide because it is needed at any point. A multi-step action is an optional process, and it is stage-only because it applies only to Investigation. An optional process is for multi-step work, not a single screen. A user action covers one screen, so it cannot hold a multi-step review.

questions.stem: An architect adds a case-wide optional action in App Studio. Where is it configured, and where do users run it?
options: Optional Actions button on the Workflow tab; the Actions menu at runtime
Process Modeler of each process; the user's worklist at runtime
Settings tab of the case type; the Utilities pane at runtime
UX tab of the case type; a button added to every View
questions.explanation: You configure optional actions with the Optional Actions button in the upper right of the Workflow tab, and users run them from the Actions menu. The Settings tab holds settings such as goals and deadlines, and the Utilities pane holds widgets. The Process Modeler edits a process diagram. A promoted action appears as a header button without a button component being added, so optional actions are not placed on Views.

questions.stem: An architect is reviewing optional actions for a Claim case type. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Only user actions, not optional processes, can be promoted.
An optional process can be promoted if it is listed first in the stage.
Edit details and Change Stage are built-in case-wide actions.
Stage-only actions appear in the Actions menu throughout the case.
questions.explanation: Edit details and Change Stage are the built-in case-wide actions, and only user actions can become the promoted action. Being listed first does not let an optional process be promoted. Stage-only actions are available only in their own stage, not throughout the case.

questions.stem: After the 'Review claim' step, suspicious claims must go to an Investigation alternate stage, and all other claims continue in the current process. How should the architect model this?
options: A Decision shape whose suspicious path uses a Change to a Stage step
A Start process when condition on the Review process
A stage transition on the Create stage that checks the flag
A Skip stage when condition on the Investigation stage
questions.explanation: A Decision shape creates conditional paths, and a Change to a Stage step on one path sends the case to another stage, including an alternate stage. Skip stage when only decides whether the case skips a stage; it does not send a case to an alternate stage. Start process when decides whether a whole process runs, not which way to go after a step. Transitions cannot be configured on the Create stage.

questions.stem: The business wants to change the auto-approval monetary limit several times a year without changing the process. Which two designs meet this? (Choose Two)
options: Store the limit in a Dynamic System Setting that configuration sets extend.
Hold the limit in a decision table delegated to the process owner.
Enter the limit directly in the Decision shape's condition.
Reference a configuration setting for the limit in the Condition Builder.
questions.explanation: Configuration settings parameterize process paths, such as an approval limit, and the Condition Builder can reference them. A delegated decision table lets a process owner make small changes in production, such as a threshold. Configuration sets replace Dynamic System Settings rather than extend them. A value typed into the condition needs a process change every time it changes.

questions.stem: While working on the 'Prepare quote' assignment, agents sometimes record a callback note. This must not complete the assignment or move the case forward. How should the note action be configured?
options: As a new Collect information step after Prepare quote
As a connector action on the outgoing connector
As a Wait step with a timer on the assignment
As a local action in the assignment's properties
questions.explanation: A local action updates the assignment without moving it forward, and you configure it in the assignment's properties. A connector action completes the assignment and advances the flow. A new step would make the note a required, separate step. A Wait step pauses the case and does not give the user an action to take.

questions.stem: The 'Review order' assignment has two outgoing connectors, Approve and Request changes, and a local action, Add note. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Add note advances the flow once the user submits it.
Each connector action completes the assignment and advances the flow.
A flow action defines what a user can do at a step.
Connector actions are configured in the assignment's properties.
questions.explanation: Flow actions define what a user can do at a step. A connector action completes the assignment and follows its connector. A local action such as Add note updates the assignment without advancing it. You configure local actions, not connector actions, in the assignment's properties; connector actions belong to the connectors.

questions.stem: Purchase case PP-55 creates Inspection child cases in stage 2. In stage 4 it must pause until every Inspection is resolved, however it was resolved. Some may already be Resolved-Completed. Which Wait step configuration fits?
options: Case dependency on any Inspection reaching Resolved-Completed
Timer referencing the date of the last inspection
Case dependency on all Inspections, To be resolved, checking current status
Case dependency on all Inspections, Resolved-Completed, checking only later changes
questions.explanation: To be resolved matches any status that starts with Resolved, and All waits for every child. Checking the current status counts children that were resolved before the case reached the wait. The any option resumes after one child. Checking only later changes would miss children that were already resolved, and it also leaves out other Resolved statuses. A timer has nothing to do with the children's status.

questions.stem: In case ORD-77, a Wait step for Shipment child cases runs, but the Create Case step that creates the Shipments comes later in the process. What happens at the Wait step?
options: The Wait step switches to a timer wait.
The case waits until Shipment child cases are created.
The Wait step is skipped because no child cases exist yet.
The case waits until a user cancels the wait.
questions.explanation: A case dependency wait needs the child cases to exist before it runs; if they do not, the wait is skipped. It does not wait for future children, does not change into a timer, and does not hold the case waiting for someone to cancel.

questions.stem: An architect is choosing between Wait step types. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: A Wait step is needed to pause until a user completes an assignment.
A case dependency wait can let a user cancel the wait.
A timer wait ends early when its children reach To be resolved.
A timer wait can reference a date/time property on the case.
questions.explanation: A timer can use a set interval or a referenced date/time property. A case dependency can let a user cancel the wait. To be resolved is a case dependency setting, not a timer setting. A case already waits for a user to act on an assignment, so that delay is not a Wait step.

questions.stem: A Recall case creates three Supplier Notice child cases. The parent may continue as soon as any supplier confirms, which resolves that child as Resolved-Completed. Which Wait step configuration fits?
options: Case dependency on any Supplier Notice reaching To be resolved
Timer set to an interval long enough for one reply
Case dependency on any Supplier Notice reaching Resolved-Completed
Case dependency on all Supplier Notices reaching Resolved-Completed
questions.explanation: Any with Resolved-Completed resumes the parent as soon as one supplier confirms. All would wait for every supplier. To be resolved matches every status that starts with Resolved, so a rejected or cancelled notice would also resume the parent. A timer cannot tell whether anyone replied.

questions.stem: A Review stage has two 'Skip stage when' conditions: Order total < 100 and Customer tier = Gold. ORD-1 is $80 and Silver, ORD-2 is $150 and Gold, and ORD-3 is $60 and Gold. Which orders skip the stage?
options: All three orders
ORD-2 and ORD-3
ORD-3 only
ORD-1 and ORD-3
questions.explanation: When several conditions are listed, all of them must be true (AND). Only ORD-3 is both under 100 and Gold. ORD-1 meets only the total condition, and ORD-2 meets only the tier condition. Treating the conditions as OR would wrongly skip all three.

questions.stem: In a Hiring case, the Background Check stage applies only to external candidates. In the Review stage, a Reference Check process runs only for senior roles. Which two configurations are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Nothing on Background Check, because stages are skipped by default
A Skip stage when condition on Background Check for internal candidates
A Start process when condition on Reference Check for senior roles
A Skip process when condition on Reference Check for senior roles
questions.explanation: A stage is never skipped by default, so Background Check needs a Skip stage when condition for the cases that should not enter it. A process always starts by default, so Reference Check needs a Start process when condition for the cases that should run it. Processes use Start process when, and skipping for senior roles would reverse the requirement anyway.

questions.stem: An Audit process has the condition 'Start process when Claim amount > 5000'. Claim CL-9 is for 3000. What happens to the Audit process for CL-9?
options: Audit starts anyway, because processes always start by default.
Audit starts and is then resolved automatically.
The Audit process does not start for CL-9.
The whole stage containing Audit is skipped for CL-9.
questions.explanation: A process always starts unless it has a condition. Here the condition is false, so Audit does not start. A process condition affects only that process, not its stage. The default to always start applies only when no condition is set. No automatic resolution is involved.

questions.stem: An architect is designing an Auto Claim case type. In which two situations is a child case the right choice? (Choose Two)
options: Body Injury work that other claim case types also need
A single review screen the adjuster completes before payment
A form section that collects the driver's details
Repair work done by another party on a different time frame
questions.explanation: Child cases suit work that several case types share, work done by different parties or on different time frames, separate reporting, and parallel processing. A single review screen is an assignment step. Collecting driver details is a form, not a separate piece of work.

questions.stem: A Business Trip parent case creates Hotel Booking child cases. The trip itinerary on the parent changes often, and every child must always show the current itinerary. Which approach should the architect use?
options: Have each child reference the parent's itinerary data
Copy the itinerary into each child when it is created
Add a Wait step to each child until the itinerary is final
Create each Hotel Booking as a top-level case
questions.explanation: When data must stay in sync, the child should reference the parent's data, which is an advanced Dev Studio setup. Copying gives a snapshot from creation time that goes stale when the itinerary changes. A Wait step only delays the child and does not keep data in sync. A top-level case has no parent to read from.

questions.stem: An Accident Claim parent creates a Vehicle Damage child that copies the accident details when it is created. The parent's accident description is corrected later. What does the child show?
options: No description, because children cannot use parent data
Both descriptions, kept in the child's case history
The original description copied when the child was created
The corrected description, because children always read parent data
questions.explanation: Copying data at creation takes a snapshot, so later changes on the parent do not reach the child. Children read live parent data only when they are set to reference it. The child does not keep both values. Children can receive parent data, by copy or by reference.

questions.stem: An architect is configuring child cases for a Mortgage case type. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Choosing a top-level case instead of a child is configured in Dev Studio.
A top-level case becomes the parent of the case that created it.
Creating several child cases in one step is an App Studio-only option.
The parent case cannot be resolved until its child cases are resolved.
questions.explanation: Dev Studio offers the choice between a top-level case and a child case, and the option to create multiple child cases. The parent must wait for its children to be resolved before it can be resolved. Creating multiple child cases is configured in Dev Studio, not App Studio. A top-level case has no parent and is not a child of the case that created it.

questions.stem: After 'Capture shipping', the system must copy the shipping address to billing, alert the customer by email and push notification in one step, and move the case into the Fulfillment stage. Which three automation steps are needed? (Choose Three)
options: Run Data Transform
Send notification
Change to a Stage
Send email
questions.explanation: Run Data Transform copies the shipping address into the billing fields. Send notification reaches several channels, such as email and push, in one step. Change to a Stage moves the case directly into Fulfillment. Send email covers only email, so the push notification would be missed.

questions.stem: A quick-quote case is created as a temporary case so that abandoned quotes are not stored. If the customer accepts, the case must be kept permanently. Which automation step does this?
options: Persist Case
Update a Case
Create Case
Change to next Stage
questions.explanation: Persist Case turns a temporary case into a permanent one. Create Case starts a new case. Update a Case sets values on the current case or on its child and descendant cases. Change to next Stage moves the case forward but does not make it permanent.

questions.stem: When a Recall case is cancelled, a field on all of its child and descendant cases must be set to 'Recalled'. Which automation step does this?
options: Create Case with the field prefilled
Update a Case, targeting all child and descendant cases
Run Data Transform on the Recall case
Post to Pulse on each child case
questions.explanation: Update a Case can update the current case or all of its child and descendant cases. A Run Data Transform on the Recall case changes only that case. Create Case would make new cases instead of updating the existing ones. Post to Pulse sends a message and does not change field values.

questions.stem: A pricing decision table has, in order: Row 1, UnitPrice < 50 returns Standard. Row 2, UnitPrice < 25 returns Budget. Otherwise returns Premium. The architect clicks Show conflicts. What is reported?
options: Row 2 is unreachable, because Row 1 catches every price under 25.
Nothing, because the most specific row is evaluated first.
Row 1 is unreachable, because Row 2 is more specific.
The table is incomplete, because it has no Otherwise result.
questions.explanation: Rows are evaluated from top to bottom, and the first row whose conditions are all true wins. Every price under 25 is also under 50, so Row 1 always matches first and Row 2 can never be reached. Pega does not reorder rows by how specific they are. The table does have an Otherwise result. Row 1 is reachable for prices from 25 to 49.

questions.stem: Gold customers' discount depends on region, Silver customers' discount depends on the number of past orders, and Bronze customers always get 0%. Which rule type fits best, and why?
options: A decision table, because it handles nested conditions best
A When rule, because each result is a yes or no
A decision table with Evaluate all rows to fill empty cells
A decision tree, because conditions use different properties
questions.explanation: A tree suits nested conditions that depend on different properties, and a table built for this logic would be full of empty cells. Tables suit the same set of properties evaluated across many combinations. A When rule returns only true or false, not a discount. Evaluate all rows returns every matching row; it does not fill empty cells.

questions.stem: A Shipping case type uses a decision table to choose the shipping method. The process owner must adjust thresholds in production. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Turning on Evaluate all rows keeps Allowed to return values enabled.
Delegation options on the Results tab control what the owner can change.
Show conflicts still reports unreachable rows with Evaluate all rows on.
Rows are evaluated top to bottom, and the first fully true row returns.
questions.explanation: A table returns the first row from the top whose conditions are all true. You set delegation options on the Results tab, for example allowing the owner to add columns but not rows. Evaluate all rows disables Allowed to return values. With Evaluate all rows on, no conflicts are reported because every row is checked.

questions.stem: An architect is choosing between a decision table and a decision tree. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: A tree is preferred when every condition uses the same properties.
Show completeness adds rows for missing cases, and the user decides which to keep.
An authority matrix cascading approval supports only decision tables.
Using a tree for table-shaped logic leaves many empty cells.
questions.explanation: Authority matrix approvals work only with decision tables. Show completeness adds rows for missing conditions, which can be many, and the user decides what to keep. When the conditions use the same properties, a table is the better choice. Empty cells come from forcing tree-shaped logic into a table; forcing table-shaped logic into a tree causes repeated conditions instead.

questions.stem: Citizen developers in App Studio cannot select a decision table built in Dev Studio when they configure a calculated field. What is the most likely cause?
options: Calculated fields support only functions and expressions.
The table must first be saved into the Work- class.
The decision table is not marked as a relevant record.
Decision tables can be referenced only from Dev Studio.
questions.explanation: A Dev Studio decision table appears in App Studio only after it is marked as a relevant record. App Studio calculated fields can use decision tables, along with functions and expressions. Tables created in App Studio are stored in a Work- class, but the class is not what controls visibility; the relevant record mark does.

questions.stem: In the lifecycle's Personas & Channels section, the architect drafted that the Manager persona uses only the Manager Portal. In testing, managers can still open every page of the Web Portal. What is the fix?
options: Assign the Manager persona when configuring the Manager Portal.
Create a new Access Role for the persona in App Studio.
Remove the Web Portal, because personas cannot share channels.
Set persona and channel access on the Create stage only.
questions.explanation: Drafting personas and channels in the lifecycle does not set channel access, and by default a persona can reach all pages. You restrict a portal by assigning the persona when you configure that portal. Access Roles are a Dev Studio concept and do not fix the drafting gap. Persona and channel access can be set per stage, not only on the Create stage. Personas can share channels.

questions.stem: An architect creates a new 'Claims Supervisor' persona in App Studio. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: An Access Group is created automatically for the persona.
Every Access Role in Dev Studio has a matching persona.
Creating an Access Group in Dev Studio creates a matching persona.
Default permissions and a work queue are created for the persona.
questions.explanation: Creating a persona creates default permissions, a work queue and an Access Group. It does not work the other way: creating an Access Group does not create a persona. Each persona is linked to a role, but not every role has a persona.
